Five consecutive victories, 113 attempts on goal, eight different scorers and a historic triumph over defending champions DPR Korea have propelled Nigeria to the final of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup .
Now, Akeem Busari’s Flamingos are 90 minutes away from becoming the first African nation to lift the trophy.
There is something remarkable about the way Nigeria’s Flamingos have transformed their FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup campaign in Morocco.
From the disappointment of losing their opening match against Poland to delivering one of the tournament’s most impressive attacking performances against Brazil, Akeem Busari’s youngsters have shown the resilience, ambition and quality to compete for the biggest prize in youth women’s football.
Their journey has been a story of redemption, collective responsibility and an increasingly convincing belief that they belong among the world’s best.
But as Nigeria prepare to face Japan in the final, the numbers behind their campaign tell an even more compelling story.
They reveal a Nigerian team that has been relentless in attack, dangerous from different positions, capable of recovering from adversity and increasingly comfortable against opponents with established international pedigrees.

Japan, however, arrive with a history of their own. The Asian powerhouse are preparing for a fourth final appearance, having established themselves as one of the competition’s most successful nations.
The numbers surrounding Saturday’s showdown provide a fascinating picture of what is at stake, with records, individual breakthroughs and national pride all converging on one decisive occasion.
Japan’s remarkable attacking history at the U-17 Women’s World Cup reached another milestone in their semi-final against DPR Korea.
Their dramatic last-gasp equaliser, which came through an own goal by Won Sol-gyong, took their all-time goals tally in the competition to 150.
That figure places Japan comfortably above every other nation in the tournament’s history, with a 26-goal advantage over their fellow Asian powerhouses, DPR Korea.
It is a testament to Japan’s longevity and attacking philosophy that it has consistently produced technically gifted players capable of making an impact on the global stage.
However, Nigeria have developed their own attacking identity in Morocco, and their numbers suggest Japan will face a significant examination in the final.
The Flamingos have registered 113 attempts on goal, the second-highest tally in the competition, behind only DPR Korea’s 186.
More impressively, 35 of those attempts came in their semi-final victory over Brazil, underlining the intensity with which Busari’s team approached one of their biggest matches of the tournament.
That performance was not simply about scoring goals. It showed Nigeria’s willingness to attack, sustain pressure, and repeatedly test an opponent’s defensive organisation.
Against a Japanese side that has conceded only twice throughout the tournament, the Flamingos will need to translate their attacking volume into clinical finishing.
One of the most compelling individual stories from Nigeria’s journey is Awawu Bashiru.
Before the semi-final against Brazil, the youngster had accumulated just 73 minutes of playing time, with every minute coming after being introduced from the bench.
Yet, when the opportunity arrived against Brazil, Bashiru delivered arguably the most decisive performance of her tournament.
She scored twice to help Nigeria secure their place in the final and was named Player of the Match.
Her emergence highlighted something important about this Flamingos squad: the ability to find match-winners beyond the regular starting personnel.
At a tournament where fatigue, tactical adjustments and squad depth can determine how far a team progresses, Bashiru’s contribution could prove invaluable.
For Nigeria, her performance also represents the importance of patience and readiness. Having spent much of the competition waiting for her opportunity, she seized it when the stakes were highest.
The semi-final may well be remembered as the moment Bashiru announced herself on the international stage.
Nigeria’s attacking threat has not depended on one individual, and the tournament’s goalscoring statistics show the collective responsibility within Busari’s team.
Eight different players have found the net in Morocco; Oluwakemi Adegbuyi, Awawu Bashiru, Oluebube Umejiaku and Kanyinsola Yusuf have scored twice each, while Mary Dunstan, Queen Joseph, Azeezat Oduntan and Precious Oscar have each contributed one goal.
That distribution is particularly encouraging heading into the final.
Japan will have to prepare for several potential attacking threats rather than concentrating exclusively on stopping one prolific forward.
It also reflects the depth of Nigeria’s attacking options and the willingness of players from different positions to contribute to the team’s overall objectives.
For an African side seeking its first world title at this level, having multiple goalscoring outlets could be one of the most important weapons against Japan.
Perhaps nothing captures Nigeria’s journey better than their transformation from opening-match disappointment to finalists.
The Flamingos began their Morocco 2026 campaign with a 2-1 defeat to Poland, an outcome that immediately placed pressure on the team and complicated their route through the group.
However, rather than allowing that setback to define their tournament, Busari’s players responded with five consecutive victories.
Their recovery has been particularly impressive because it required more than simply collecting points. They had to rebuild confidence, improve their performances and negotiate increasingly difficult challenges.
Their victories over subsequent opponents, including defending champions DPR Korea, and their elimination of Brazil in the semi-finals demonstrated how much the team had grown since that opening defeat.
Japan have also won their last five matches, meaning both finalists arrive at the showpiece with identical winning streaks.
Those five successive victories represent the fourth-longest winning sequence in the competition’s history.
Only Japan’s extraordinary 11-match run between 2014 and 2016, Spain’s nine victories between 2022 and 2024, and DPR Korea’s nine-match sequence spanning 2025 and 2026 rank higher.
Yet Nigeria’s achievement carries a particularly interesting dimension: they are now chasing a title after losing their opening fixture, something no previous champion has accomplished.
A victory over Japan would therefore add another chapter to tournament history.
Before the semi-final triumph over Brazil, one of the defining moments of Nigeria’s campaign was their group-stage victory over defending champions DPR Korea.
By defeating the holders in regulation time, the Flamingos became the first nation to beat a defending champion in regulation time at a U-17 Women’s World Cup final.
That achievement was significant beyond the three points it delivered as DPR Korea entered Morocco with the reputation of champions and the experience of a team accustomed to dominating youth women’s football.
Nigeria, however, refused to be intimidated by that pedigree. The victory showed that Busari’s team had the tactical discipline and competitive mentality to challenge the best, providing a major confidence boost ahead of the knockout stages.
It was also an important statement for African football, reinforcing the continent’s ability to produce teams that can upset established global powers.
While Nigeria’s story has been built around their remarkable recovery, Japan’s journey reflects consistency and an established tradition of excellence.
The final will be Japan’s 50th match in the competition’s history, a milestone that underscores their remarkable longevity.
Only DPR Korea will have played more matches, reaching 51 appearances when they face Brazil in the third-place playoff.
Japan are also preparing for their fourth final, having previously reached the championship match in 2010, 2014 and 2016.
Their only previous triumph came at the 2014 Costa Rica tournament, when they defeated Spain 2-0 in San Jose to become world champions.
Their presence at every edition of the tournament since its inception further underscores their remarkable consistency. Alongside New Zealand, Japan are the only nation to have featured in all 10 editions.
That experience is reflected in the technical quality and tactical organisation they have displayed in Morocco.
For Nigeria, beating such an established opponent would make the achievement even more significant.
Japan’s head coach, Sadayoshi Shirai, will also reach a personal milestone in the final.
The encounter will be his 16th appearance as a coach at the U-17 Women’s World Cup, making him the most experienced coach in the competition’s history by matches managed.
Having guided Japan at the previous two editions, Shirai has now taken his team to another final, further strengthening his reputation within the tournament.
His experience will be an important advantage, particularly in a match where tactical decisions and pressure management could determine the outcome.
Busari, meanwhile, has an opportunity to write a completely different kind of history. The Nigerian coach has guided the Flamingos through a difficult opening, a challenging group campaign, and two major knockout examinations to bring them within touching distance of the trophy.
For him, the final is a chance to deliver a historic achievement for Nigeria and African women’s football.
If Nigeria’s attacking numbers are impressive, Japan’s defensive statistics are equally revealing. The Asian side has conceded only twice on their way to the final, against Kenya and DPR Korea.
At the corresponding stage of the competition, only two teams have recorded better defensive numbers: DPR Korea in 2024 and Japan themselves in 2014.
Both sides conceded fewer goals, although they had played one match less than the current finalists at that stage.
That defensive resilience presents a fascinating contrast with Nigeria’s attacking ambition. The Flamingos have shown they can create chances in large numbers, but Japan have shown an ability to restrict opponents and protect their goal.
The final could therefore become a contest between Nigeria’s attacking persistence and Japan’s defensive discipline.
For Busari’s team, converting chances will be crucial. Creating 35 attempts against Brazil was impressive, but the final demands greater efficiency against an opponent that has conceded very little throughout the tournament.
Beyond the impressive statistics and individual milestones, the biggest story remains Nigeria’s opportunity to bring the U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy to Africa for the first time.
The Flamingos have carried the continent’s hopes with distinction, demonstrating that African women’s football has the talent and competitive quality to challenge the traditional powerhouses.
Nigeria’s reputation as a producer of elite female football talent is well established, but a world title at this level would provide another important landmark for the country’s youth development system.
It would also send a powerful message to young African girls who dream of competing on the global stage.
Japan have history, experience and an impressive defensive record. Nigeria have momentum, attacking depth and the confidence gained from eliminating the defending champions and Brazil.
The Flamingos have already overcome the disappointment of their opening defeat, produced 113 attempts on goal, found match-winners from the bench, and shown they can compete with the world’s best.
Five consecutive victories have brought Nigeria to the doorstep of history. A sixth would not just deliver the country’s first U-17 Women’s World Cup title; it would establish a new landmark for African women’s football.
For Busari and his players, Morocco 2026 has become more than a tournament. It is a chance to turn an extraordinary journey into an unforgettable chapter in Nigerian and African football history.
